opus-5.5.text:
I think it's reasonable because a demo and a deployed product are solving fundamentally different problems. A demo only has to work once, maybe in front of a camera, maybe after twenty takes, in an environment you've carefully set up. Deployment has to work thousands of times a day, in places you've never seen, with people who don't care about your research and just want the task done. The gap between those two is enormous.

If you look at the history of other technologies, this timeline isn't unusual at all. Self-driving cars are a good example. The DARPA challenges in the mid-2000s showed cars could drive themselves, and it took well over a decade before you had robotaxis carrying paying passengers in a few cities. And driving is in some ways a narrower problem than general manipulation. With robots, you're touching the physical world directly. Objects are deformable, they slip, lighting changes, a cup is a slightly different shape. Every one of those long-tail cases is something the system has to handle reliably, not just most of the time.

Then there's the reliability bar itself. In a research setting, if your success rate goes from 60 percent to 85 percent, that's a great paper. But in a factory or a home, 85 percent means the robot fails constantly, and somebody has to come fix it. Getting from 85 to 99, and then to 99.9, is where most of the engineering effort goes, and each additional nine tends to be as hard as everything before it.

And it's not only the AI. You need hardware that's durable and cheap enough, that doesn't break after a few hundred hours. You need safety certification, maintenance, supply chains, a business model where the robot actually saves someone money. All of that matures in parallel, and it takes time.

So when I say five to ten years, I'm actually quite optimistic. The progress we've seen recently with foundation models, with learning from large-scale data, has really accelerated things. The demos today are much more general than they were even three years ago. But I think it's healthy for the field to be honest that the demo is the beginning of the journey, not the end. If we set expectations that it'll be in every home next year, we risk disappointment and a backlash, and that hurts everyone working on this.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the gap between what a demo proves and what deployment requires. A demo shows that something is possible once, under conditions you've chosen. Deployment means it works thousands of times, in conditions you didn't choose, and when it fails, it fails safely.

If you look at the history of other technologies, this timeline is actually normal. Self-driving cars had impressive demos in the DARPA challenges around 2005, 2007, and it took well over a decade before you could ride in one as a paying customer in a city. Speech recognition worked in the lab long before it worked on your phone in a noisy street. Robotics is harder than both of those in some ways, because the robot physically touches the world. A mistake isn't a wrong word, it's a dropped cup or a damaged shelf or, in the worst case, someone getting hurt.

So concretely, what fills those five to ten years? A few things. First, the long tail. In the lab we might cover ninety percent of situations, and the last ten percent is what the real world is mostly made of. Every home is different, lighting changes, objects are in unexpected places. Second, reliability. A demo at ninety-five percent success looks amazing in a video, but if a robot fails one in twenty times in your kitchen, you'll stop using it within a week. Getting to ninety-nine point something is not incremental work, it often requires rethinking the whole system. Third, cost and hardware. The robots we use in research are expensive and fragile. Making them affordable and durable enough that a company can actually sell them is its own engineering journey. And fourth, you need the data flywheel. Once robots are out there, you collect data from real usage, retrain, redeploy. That loop takes time to spin up.

I'd also say five to ten years is not pessimistic, it's realistic, and in some sense it's exciting, because the progress in learning-based methods, especially with large models and simulation, has compressed what used to be twenty-year problems. When I started, many people thought learning-based locomotion would never run on real hardware. Now it's standard. So I'm optimistic, I just think we should be honest about the distance between a great video and a product in your home.

astra-6.text:
I think a demo and a deployed product answer very different questions. A demo shows that something is possible under a particular set of conditions. Deployment means it works reliably across all the conditions your customers encounter, at a cost they can afford.

In robotics, that gap is especially large because you’re interacting with the physical world. Lighting changes, objects move, hardware wears out, and people do things you didn’t anticipate. A robot that succeeds most of the time can look impressive in a demo, but if someone has to intervene every hour, it may not be useful in practice. You also need to solve safety, manufacturing, maintenance, and integration into an existing workflow.

Those things take iteration: put robots in the field, discover failures, improve the system, and test again. So five to ten years doesn’t strike me as unreasonable, particularly for a new category of robot. It’s not a fixed rule, but proving that something can work is a very different milestone from making it dependable enough that someone will build their business around it.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a demo and a deployed product have very different requirements. In a demo, you can control the environment, and you only need the robot to succeed a few times. In deployment, it has to work reliably every day, under conditions you didn’t anticipate. When it fails, it needs to fail safely, and someone needs to be able to maintain it at a reasonable cost.

That means you’re not just improving an algorithm. You’re improving the hardware, collecting data, finding failure cases, and integrating the whole system into an actual workflow. A lot of those problems only become visible when you put robots in the field. So five to ten years can be a reasonable engineering timeline. The demo shows that something is possible; deployment requires making it consistently useful.
